title: 'Kids literally disappeared': Minnesota schools lost at least 1,700 students following Operation Metro Surge
author: Becky Z. Dernbach and Cynthia Tu
summary: This Sahan Journal investigation quantifies a phenomenon Minnesota school administrators had been describing anecdotally: a sudden, unprecedented wave of student disappearances tied to federal immigration enforcement. Analyzing data from 29 districts and charter schools, reporters Becky Z. Dernbach and Cynthia Tu found roughly 1,700 students left school rolls between October 2025 and March 2026 — more than twenty times the prior year's typical midyear decline — with Minneapolis and St. Paul each losing close to 500 students. The piece traces the exodus to two compounding forces: restrictive federal immigration policy beginning in January 2025, and Operation Metro Surge, a spring 2026 enforcement campaign that detained more than 3,400 people including at least 70 children. Crucially, the reporting distinguishes between families who visibly relocated and a second, harder-to-track group: students marked absent for 15 consecutive days who simply never resurfaced in any school system, a category that tripled during the surge. The investigation closes on a concrete institutional consequence — St. Paul's elimination of 16.3 English-language-teacher positions — showing how the enrollment shock is now reshaping staffing for the very students the cuts affect most.
points: The scale comparison — roughly 1,700 students lost in one enforcement-affected period versus fewer than 80 in the prior year's typical midyear decline — turns an anecdotal impression among superintendents into a quantified, historically unprecedented enrollment shock.

The reporting's distinction between families who relocated and the tripled cohort of students who vanished after 15 consecutive absences and never resurfaced anywhere reveals a second, harder-to-measure form of educational loss beyond simple district-to-district transfer.

By connecting the enrollment collapse directly to St. Paul's elimination of 16.3 English-language-teacher positions, the story shows the fiscal feedback loop: enforcement drives away the highest-need students, and the resulting budget cuts then reduce services for those who remain.
